planet.sun.description: The Sun is a star made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It gives Earth light and heat.
planet.mercury.description: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It completes an orbit in about 88 Earth days.
planet.venus.description: Venus has a thick atmosphere that traps heat. Its surface is hotter than Mercury’s, even though it is farther from the Sun.
planet.earth.description: Earth has liquid water and an atmosphere that supports life. It takes about 365 days to travel around the Sun.
planet.mars.description: Mars is a rocky planet with reddish dust. Its day is a little longer than Earth’s, but its year is almost twice as long.
planet.jupiter.description: Jupiter is the largest planet. Its colourful bands are clouds, and the Great Red Spot is a huge storm.
planet.saturn.description: Saturn is a gas giant. Its rings are made of many pieces of ice and rock, not one solid sheet.
planet.uranus.tagline: A planet tilted on its side
planet.uranus.description: Uranus is an ice giant. Its axis is tilted so far that the planet appears to spin on its side.
planet.neptune.description: Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun. One orbit takes about 165 Earth years.

¹ Rounded reference values. Giant-planet: ¹ Rounded reference values. Giant-planet measurements refer to atmospheric levels, not solid ground.
Planet positions use NASA/JPL orbital el: Planet positions use NASA/JPL orbital elements. Their paths are ellipses (slightly stretched circles), tilted at different angles.
AU is a distance unit: 1 AU is about the: AU is a distance unit: 1 AU is about the average distance from Earth to the Sun. A light-minute is the distance light travels in one minute. These positions are approximate, not suitable for spacecraft navigation.
Rotation is measured relative to the sta: Rotation is measured relative to the stars. The discs do not show distance or atmospheric detail.
The Sun is a star, not a planet. Fusion: The Sun is a star, not a planet. Fusion in its core releases energy that eventually reaches the surface and travels into space as light. Different solar latitudes rotate at different speeds.
Compare the Sun with Earth. Even with en: Compare the Sun with Earth. Even with enlarged planets, this display compresses the enormous difference in their sizes.
Rotation and a solar day are different m: Rotation and a solar day are different measurements. Mercury turns once relative to the stars in about 59 Earth days, but the Sun takes about 176 Earth days to return to the same place in its sky.
Set the clock to 88 days. Mercury comple: Set the clock to 88 days. Mercury completes approximately one orbit while Earth has travelled only part of the way around.
Venus rotates in the opposite direction: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to Earth. Its dense atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter at the surface than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. This model uses a surface texture, with the clouds removed.
Compare its rotation period with its yea: Compare its rotation period with its year: a full turn relative to the stars takes longer than one orbit.
Earth’s tilted axis produces the seasons: Earth’s tilted axis produces the seasons as it travels around the Sun. A rotation relative to distant stars takes about 23 hours 56 minutes; a solar day is slightly longer because Earth also moves along its orbit.
Jump forward 182.625 days to move about: Jump forward 182.625 days to move about halfway around the orbit. Notice that the tilted spin axis keeps the same orientation in space.
A Martian solar day, called a sol, is a: A Martian solar day, called a sol, is a little longer than an Earth day. Mars also has seasons because its axis is tilted. Surface channels and minerals preserve clues to an ancient, wetter environment.
Compare Earth and Mars. Their days and a: Compare Earth and Mars. Their days and axial tilts are similar, but a Martian year is almost twice as long.
Jupiter has no solid surface like Earth’: Jupiter has no solid surface like Earth’s. Its visible bands are clouds in a deep atmosphere. Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto orbit independently of the planet’s fast rotation.
Slow time to one hour per second and foc: Slow time to one hour per second and focus on Jupiter to watch four illustrative moon orbits. Their sizes and orbital spacing are enlarged for readability.
Saturn’s rings consist of many separate: Saturn’s rings consist of many separate pieces of ice and rock. The rings lie close to its equatorial plane, so their apparent angle changes as your viewpoint changes.
Drag above and below the planet. From th: Drag above and below the planet. From the side, the broad ring system becomes a remarkably thin line.
Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees, so: Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees, so its rotation looks almost sideways. Methane in the upper atmosphere absorbs red light, helping give the planet its blue-green appearance.
Watch the rotation axis rather than just: Watch the rotation axis rather than just the orbit. Axial tilt describes a planet’s orientation; it does not push the planet above its orbital path.
Neptune travels around the Sun much more: Neptune travels around the Sun much more slowly than Earth. Its distant atmosphere is cold but dynamic. The illustration uses enhanced blue coloring to make the planet easy to identify.
Switch to true scale to see how far apar: Switch to true scale to see how far apart the outer planets are. Select their labels to find them.

lesson.meet.title: Meet the Sun and planets
lesson.meet.curriculum: NCERT Curiosity, Grade 6, Chapter 12: Beyond Earth (2026–27), Solar System; revision for Classes 7–8.
lesson.meet.0.title: Start with the Sun
lesson.meet.0.question: What makes the Sun different from a planet?
lesson.meet.0.explanation: The Sun is a star. It gives out its own light. Planets are visible because they reflect light from the Sun.
lesson.meet.1.title: Find our home
lesson.meet.1.question: Which object do we live on? What travels around it?
lesson.meet.1.explanation: We live on Earth. The Moon travels around Earth. Earth and the other seven planets travel around the Sun.
lesson.meet.2.title: Count the planets
lesson.meet.2.question: Can the class name the eight planets in order from the Sun?
lesson.meet.2.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The gaps between them are not equal.
lesson.motion.title: A spin and a trip around the Sun
lesson.motion.curriculum: NCERT Curiosity, Grade 6, Chapter 12: Beyond Earth (2026–27), planetary motion; extension for Classes 7–8.
lesson.motion.0.title: Notice two movements
lesson.motion.0.question: Can you spot Earth spinning while it moves around the Sun? Use Pause if needed.
lesson.motion.0.explanation: Rotation means spinning. Revolution means travelling around another object. Earth does both at the same time.
lesson.motion.1.title: Compare a year
lesson.motion.1.question: Which finishes a trip around the Sun sooner: Mercury or Earth?
lesson.motion.1.explanation: Mercury takes about 88 Earth days. Earth takes about 365 days. A year means one complete trip around the Sun.
lesson.motion.2.title: Think about a longer year
lesson.motion.2.question: Why should we always say which planet we mean when we say one year?
lesson.motion.2.explanation: Each planet takes a different time to orbit the Sun. Neptune takes about 165 Earth years.
lesson.distance.title: How far does sunlight travel?
lesson.distance.curriculum: Extension activity for Classes 6–8: distances and the solar system. Not a prescribed NCERT exercise.
lesson.distance.0.title: A useful distance unit
lesson.distance.0.question: Why might we use a special unit for the space between planets?
lesson.distance.0.explanation: The numbers in kilometres are very large. One astronomical unit, or AU, is about the average distance from Earth to the Sun.
lesson.distance.1.title: Light takes time
lesson.distance.1.question: Does sunlight reach Earth instantly?
lesson.distance.1.explanation: No. Light takes about eight minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth. The exact time changes slightly as Earth moves.
lesson.distance.2.title: Try the distance journey
lesson.distance.2.question: Would sunlight take more or less time to reach Neptune?
lesson.distance.2.explanation: More time: roughly four hours. End this lesson and choose Scale Journey to see the distances and a light-time counter.

Orbit is a free, non-profit educational: Orbit is a free, non-profit educational model of the Sun and eight planets, with Earth’s Moon and four illustrative Jovian moons.
One simulation clock drives planet rotat: One simulation clock drives planet rotation and date-based elliptical orbits. Planetary tilt is independent of orbital position. Moon orbits are independent of the parent’s spin.
Planet positions use NASA/JPL J2000 elem: Planet positions use NASA/JPL J2000 elements and rates for 1800–2050. Earth represents the Earth–Moon centre of mass. UTC approximates the source’s dynamical time; time-scale corrections are omitted. Spins and moon positions remain illustrative. Overview distances are compressed. True scale uses the same physical scale for planetary distances and diameters. Labels remain large enough to select. Surface colors and lighting favor legibility; the Jovian moons share a lunar texture.
Distances and light times are calculated: Distances and light times are calculated from this model. Temperature and gravity are rounded reference values; giant planets have no solid surface. A sidereal rotation and a solar day are different measures.
